newsitem.title: GERMANY: Poehl-French view on ECB potentially catastrophic.
newsitem.headline: Poehl-French view on ECB potentially catastrophic.

text.p: Former Bundesbank head Karl Otto Poehl warned that French proposals to curb the power of the European Central Bank (ECB) ran counter to the Maastricht Treaty and may have a "catastrophic" impact on financial markets.

In an outspoken attack on demands by the French government to create a political counterweight to the ECB and to give governments a say in exchange rate policy, Poehl said such a stance showed a dangerous lack of confidence in the markets.
"These proposals are not only irreconcilable with the text of the Treaty, they also extremely dangerous," Poehl said in a written commentary published in Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung on Saturday.

"If financial markets became convinced that a European central bank could be forced by political pressure to conduct a deliberate policy of devaluing the euro against the dollar or the yen, there could be portfolio shifts of catastrophic proportions."
Hundreds of billions of marks worth of mark-denominated securities which will be converted to euros are in the hands of foreign institutions, said Poehl.
Fear of a devaluation tends to prompt investors to sell securities denominated in the currency at risk and switch into alternative currencies.
Poehl said comments from French prime minister Alain Juppe reflected "a deep mistrust in the functioning of financial markets, which however is not in line French tradition."
The debate revealed there was a "more or less concealed dissent about the sense and purpose of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU)," Poehl said.

While Germany saw the main benefit of EMU as eliminating currency risk and thereby creating a real single market, France wanted the euro as a way to counteract the dominance of the dollar and the vagaries of financial markets, Poehl said.

Poehl noted that the ECB's complete independence, approved by governments and parliaments in an addendum to the Maastricht Treaty on European Union, had been a fundamental precondition for Germany and other states agreeing to the single currency.
"It is also irritating and factually incorrect when the French side keeps asserting that exchange rate policy in a currency union is a matter for governments," Poehl said.

The statute of the ECB stated that while the choice of exchange rate systems -- such as whether to return to fixed global exchange rates -- was up to governments, exchange rate policy was the domain of the ECB, which would have adequate currency reserves to do so, Poehl said.

The ECB is due to start work as guarantor of a stable euro as soon as monetary union is launched. The scheduled starting date for EMU is January 1, 1999. Maastricht states that the ECB must be independent to ensure it can concentrate on its main task of keeping inflation down.
Poehl chaired the council of central banks that drafted the statute for the ECB during his time as Bundesbank President. He headed Germany's powerful central bank from 1980 until 1991.
His comments echo remarks made by Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer on Friday who in the text of a speech made a clear reference to comments from French president Jacques Chirac.

Using the French phrases "pouvoir politique" -- political power -- and "pouvoir monetaire" -- political power, Tietmeyer said: "Any attempts to create a 'pouvoir politique' to control or influence the 'pouvoir monetaire' would not be in line with the Treaty."
